endorsements.quote: Central to such a framework is the implementation of transparent, informed consent processes that explicitly detail the extent of AI involvement in a survivor’s clinical care or research participation.

Furthermore, researchers and clinicians must remain aware of the rapidly evolving state and federal regulations related to the use of AI in the context of mental health treatment ( Shumate et al., 2025 ; Szoke et al., 2025 ).

Predeployment strategies should include training models on diverse, representative datasets; conducting audits across demographic subgroups and trauma types to prioritize equity; implementing “jailbreaking exercises” to identify potential failures and weaknesses; and establishing independent validation processes ( Ferryman et al., 2023 ; Labkoff et al., 2024 ; Welch et al., 2026 ).

During deployment, crisis escalation protocols with defined response times must be implemented and actively monitored, “human-in-the-loop” oversight for high-risk situations must be maintained, real-time safety monitoring interfaces should be used, and defined check-ins with clinicians engaging with the AI tool should be prioritized.

Postdeployment strategies include mandating adverse event reporting systems with close oversight, conducting ongoing bias testing across diverse user groups, tracking emerging evidence and updating algorithms to align with new evidence, and performing deimplementation strategies when harms or risks are detected ( Labkoff et al., 2024 ).

To advance research in this area, AI developers should partner with expert clinicians to validate their tools for these functions.

Further, prior to clinical deployment, trauma-focused LLMs require evaluation against suitable controls to assess efficacy and effectiveness, appropriateness, safety and privacy, and impacts on clinical outcomes of interest (e.g., PTSD and/or depression reduction, improved access to mental health services).

This timeline is incongruent with the rapid pace of AI evolution, necessitating alternative and novel evaluation frameworks (e.g., hybrid effectiveness–implementation studies, A/B testing, stepped wedge designs) that balance rigor with adaptability.

The inclusion of trauma survivors as partners to co-create LLMs is crucial to gather perceptions regarding safety and privacy (e.g., comfort regarding data storage, what health information is being assessed, processes for monitoring and addressing harmful or dangerous user behaviors), engagement (e.g., relevance of content and modules, length of time spent on sample sections, overall satisfaction with the LLM), and implementation (e.g., compatibility and integration potential within existing workflows, sustainability and scalability for a wide range of trauma populations).

If AI is going to be used to promote better access for individuals who are unable or unwilling to seek traditional mental health services, efforts to increase digital and AI literacy are essential ( Camacho & Torous, 2023 ).

Moreover, it will be crucial that resource recommendations are based on clinical relevance rather than commercial interest (e.g., advertisement-based recommendations in LLMs) to ensure that trauma survivors receive the most appropriate care options.

The framework emphasizes continuous feedback and engagement from a wide range of key partners, including trauma survivors, clinicians, developers, and subject-matter experts, and proposes a tiered research agenda to advance evidence-based AI applications in trauma care.

unlisted_practices: Integrate AI into trauma treatment to augment therapists rather than replace them, retaining human-in-the-loop oversight.
Train trauma-focused LLMs on data reflecting the structures and techniques of evidence-based trauma treatments.
Validate culturally and linguistically tailored LLM responses with native speakers and community members from target populations.
Design trauma crisis protocols that distinguish therapeutic distress from crisis to avoid false alarms interrupting therapeutic progress.
Prioritize technical safeguards such as encryption, parental consent, and confidential data storage for AI tools used with children.
Develop evidence-informed guidelines and a central resource to help users evaluate the quality of AI tools for trauma treatment.
Carefully vet resources recommended by AI tools before they are suggested to users.
